abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: This phase 2, single-arm, multi-center study (NCT03934567) evaluates the efficacy and safety of abexinostat, a histone deacetylase inhibitor, in patients with relapsed or refractory (r/r) follicular lymphoma (FL). Eligible participants had previously received a minimum of two systemic treatment lines, such as cytotoxic agents and/or anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies. Participants received abexinostat 80 mg oral twice daily on a schedule of seven days on and seven days off, within 28-day cycles, continuing until unacceptable toxicity or disease progression occurred. The primary endpoint was objective response rate (ORR), evaluated by an independent review committee (IRC). Secondary endpoints comprised duration of response (DoR), disease control rate (DCR), progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), and safety. Between May 2, 2019, and November 19, 2023, 90 patients were enrolled. As of October 08, 2024, with a median follow-up of 30.55 months (95% confidence interval [CI] 23.72–33.64), 17.8% (16/90) of patients were still on study treatment. The ORR was 69.5% (57/82, 95% CI 58.4–79.2), with a complete response rate of 14.6% (12/82). The DCR was 91.5% (75/82, 95% CI 83.2–96.5). Tumor size reduced in 89% (73/82) of patients. The median DoR was 13.96 months (95% CI 9.20–not reached [NR]) and the median PFS was 13.80 months (95% CI 9.69–30.26). The median OS was 47.18 months (95% CI 45.70–NR). The most common treatment-emergent adverse events were thrombocytopenia (77/90, 85.6%), neutropenia (53/90, 58.9%), and leukopenia (47/90, 52.2%). The results of this study demonstrated that abexinostat had promising efficacy and manageable safety profile, supporting abexinostat as a new treatment option for the third-line or later-line treatment of r/r FL.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Follicular lymphoma (FL) is an indolent subtype of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL), characterized by a prolonged clinical course.1 Despite relatively slow progression, FL presents substantial treatment challenges, primarily due to its propensity to relapse and develop resistance to conventional therapies. FL typically manifests with a pattern of repeated remission and recurrence, which complicates the long-term management and adversely affects health-related quality of life.1,2 Characterized by the proliferation of follicle center B-cells, FL’s clinical behavior and response to treatment can vary significantly among patients. Epidemiological data from Western countries indicate that 20–25% of newly diagnosed NHL cases are FL, with age-adjusted incidence rates of 2–4 per 100,000 person-years.1,3 In China, FL constitutes 2.5–6.6% of NHL cases.4,5

Despite notable progress in the therapeutic management of FL across multiple lines of therapy, unmet needs persist, especially for patients with relapsed or refractory (r/r) disease. Front-line treatment commonly incorporates anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), with rituximab as a representative agent, administered either alone or in combination with chemotherapy. This approach is conducted to improve clinical outcomes, including objective response rates (ORR), progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS). Furthermore, the implementation of rituximab maintenance following initial chemo-immunotherapy has demonstrated a significant improvement in both 5-year PFS and OS compared to observation.6,7 Despite FL being typically characterized as an indolent condition with a median OS exceeding 15 years, it persists as a chronic, incurable disease. Within 24 months of starting treatment, disease progression or relapse is observed in about one-fifth of patients, underscoring a significant unmet clinical need and corresponding to a 5-year PFS rate of roughly 60%.1

Histone deacetylases (HDACs) serve as essential epigenetic regulators, modulating gene expression and influencing diverse cellular pathways vital to oncogenesis. By catalyzing histone deacetylation, HDACs promote a condensed chromatin state, which subsequently inhibits transcriptional activity.8 Disrupted histone acetylation patterns—specifically the depletion of H4K16ac and H4K20me3—are established phenotypic markers of malignancy.9 Within the context of FL, epigenetic dysregulation is a primary pathogenic driver. Nearly 90% of cases exhibit genetic lesions affecting histone-modifying enzymes, including methyltransferases (such as KMT2D and EZH2) or acetyltransferases (notably CREBBP and EP300), most of which result in loss of enzymatic function.10 Therapeutically, HDAC inhibitors may partially compensate for the reduced histone acetylation associated with CREBBP or EP300 inactivation.10,11

HDAC inhibitors, including abexinostat, are part of a broader class of compounds known for their potential in cancer therapy. To date, several agents in this class have received regulatory approval. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved vorinostat12,13 and romidepsin for the treatment of r/r cutaneous T-cell lymphoma,14,15 while belinostat is indicated for the treatment of r/r peripheral T-cell lymphoma (PTCL).16 Similarly, in China, the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) approved chidamide for treating both r/r PTCL and double-expressor diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.17–19 The ORR was 47% (8/17) for vorinostat monotherapy,20 50% (11/22) for vorinostat plus rituximab,21 and 50% (1/2) for vorinostat plus cladribine plus rituximab22 in patients with r/r FL. Abexinostat, manufactured by Xynomic Pharmaceuticals (Nanjing) Co., Ltd, Nanjing, China, represents an innovative approach that could potentially shift the treatment paradigm for r/r FL, offering new hope to those in need of alternative therapeutic options. The results of phase 1 study in Chinese patients with r/r B cell NHL demonstrated that the recommended phase 2 dose of abexinostat was 80 mg orally twice daily (bis in die, BID) one week on, one week off.23 To evaluate the efficacy and safety of abexinostat monotherapy in patients with r/r FL, we conducted this multi-center, single-arm, pivotal phase 2 study.

sec.title: Patient characteristics and treatment
sec.p: The first patient of this study was enrolled on May 2, 2019. At the time of interim analysis, the ORR was 62.2% (23/37). Thus, the study proceeded to the second stage and enrolled the last patient on Nov 19, 2023. The study enrolled 90 patients in two stages, all receiving at least one dose of abexinostat. Patients received abexinostat orally at 80 mg BID, with a 4-h interval between doses, administered in cycles of 7 consecutive treatment days followed by 7 days off within each 28-day period. Administration ceased upon unacceptable toxicity, disease progression, loss to follow-up, withdrawal of informed consent, or death (Fig. 1A). All 90 participants constituted the safety set (SS). The FAS comprised 82 patients, 6 patients were excluded due to the absence of post-baseline efficacy evaluations, and 2 patients were excluded due to inadequate prior treatment history. The second-line treatment of one patient only last 10 days and another patient had no efficacy evaluation for the whole second-line treatment due to COVID-19 pandemic. The dropout rate of this study was 9% (8/90), <15%, and was terminated after reaching the efficacy evaluation of 82 patients. 57.8% (52/90) were men, and 92.2% (83/90) were stage Ⅲ–Ⅳ. Before enrollment, patients had received median previous treatment lines of 3 (range: 2–9), and all had been exposed to anti-CD20 mAbs therapy. Following the last treatment, relapse occurred in 75.6% (68/90) of cases, while 24.4% (22/90) were refractory (Table 1).

sec.p: The median follow-up time was 30.55 months (95% confidence interval [CI] 23.72-33.64) at the October 8, 2024 cutoff. Overall, treatment discontinuation occurred in 74 of 90 patients (82.2%), with disease progression representing the leading cause (49/90, 54.4%), followed by patient withdrawal of consent (14/90, 15.6%), investigator decision (6/90, 6.7%), adverse events (3/90, 3.3%), initiation of new anticancer therapy (1/90, 1.1%), and other reasons (1/90, 1.1%). 17.8% (16/90) of patients were still on the study treatment, 46.7% (43/90) of patients were in follow-up, and 34.4% (31/90) of patients had discontinued the study (Fig. 1b).

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: Among 82 patients included in the FAS, the independent review center (IRC) assessed ORR was 69.5% (57/82, 95% CI 58.4–79.2) with 14.6% (12/82) achieving a complete response (CR). The lower bound of 95% CI of ORR was 58.4% which exceeded the prespecified threshold of 30%. Tumor size reduced in 89% (73/82) of patients (Fig. 2a). The changes in sum of the product of the perpendicular diameters (SPD) over time were illustrated in Fig. 2b. The treatment duration and response were detailed in Fig. 2c. Assessments of ORR and CR conducted by investigators showed high concordance with those assessed by IRC (Table 2). In the FAS, the IRC-assessed disease control rate (DCR) was 91.5% (75/82, 95% CI 83.2–96.5). Subgroup analyses to explore whether objective response to abexinostat varied between subgroups. The IRC-assessed ORR were 76.9% (10/13) and 52.4% (11/21) in immunohistochemistry (IHC) CREBBP (+) and IHC CREBBP (-) patients, respectively. The IRC-assessed ORR were 72.7% (8/11) and 56.5% (13/23) in IHC KMT2D (+) and IHC KMT2D (-) patients, respectively. The IRC-assessed ORR was 69.6% (16/23) and 69.6% (41/59) in patients who had previously received and not received PI3K inhibitors, respectively (Fig. 2d).

sec.p: The IRC-assessed median duration of response (DoR) was 13.96 months (95% CI, 9.2–not reached [NR]) (Table 2, Fig. 3a). Median PFS was 13.80 months (95% CI, 9.69–30.26; Fig. 3b); with the corresponding 12-month, 24-month and 36-month PFS rates of 55.3% (95% CI, 42.5–66.3), 39.2% (95% CI, 25.9–52.2) and 33.6% (95% CI, 19.0–48.8), respectively (Table 2). Median OS was 47.18 months (95% CI, 45.70–NR) (Fig. 3c), with 12-month, 24-month, and 45-month OS rates of 95.1% (95% CI, 87.5–98.1), 85.8% (95% CI, 72.1–90.8), and 74.0% (95% CI, 59.5–83.9), respectively (Table 2). Subgroup analyses to explore whether PFS to abexinostat varied between subgroups. The IRC-assessed median PFS was 11.07 months (95% CI 2.79–NE) and not reached in IHC CREBBP (+) and IHC CREBBP (-) patients, respectively. The IRC-assessed median PFS was not reached and 13.77 months (95% CI 2.79–NE) in IHC KMT2D (+) and IHC KMT2D (-) patients, respectively. The IRC-assessed median PFS was 8.25 months (95% CI 2.79–16.72) and 15.38 months (95% CI 11.04–NE) in patients who had previously received and not received PI3K inhibitors, respectively (Fig. 3d).

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: In the SS, thrombocytopenia was the highest incidence of treatment-emergent adverse event (TEAE), observed in 77 of 90 patients (85.6%), followed by neutropenia (53/90, 58.9%) and leukopenia (47/90, 52.2%). Grade 3–4 TEAEs included thrombocytopenia (38/90, 42.2%), neutropenia (23/90, 25.6%), leukopenia (7/90, 7.8%), lymphopenia (5/90, 5.6%), hypokalemia (5/90, 5.6%), diarrhea (4/90, 4.4%), and anemia (4/90, 4.4%) (Table 3). 24.4% (22/90) of patients had a serious adverse event (SAE). One patient died from subarachnoid hemorrhage and one died from coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) infection, both events were considered unrelated to abexinostat. 3.3% (3/90) of patients discontinued study treatment due to TEAEs, including one patient who had grade 4 thrombocytopenia considered related to abexinostat, one patient died from subarachnoid hemorrhage unrelated to abexinostat, and one patient died from COVID-19 infection unrelated to abexinostat. No treatment-related death occurred.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: HDAC inhibitors represent a significant advancement for the treatment of NHL.11 In the United States, vorinostat, romidepsin, belinostat, and panobinostat are FDA-approved for r/r T-cell lymphoma, whereas in China, chidamide has gained approval from the China NMPA for this indication. Abnormal expression of HDACs has been closely linked to the pathogenesis and proliferation of cancer cells.8 HDAC inhibitors can activate tumor suppressor genes and other cell cycle-regulating genes, thereby manifesting anti-cancer activities.24

Abexinostat, a pan-HDAC inhibitor, facilitates sufficient pharmacodynamic activity while reducing peak drug concentrations to decrease toxicity.25–27 The terminal elimination half-life of abexinostat after oral administration was around 4 h. In previous clinical studies, the regimen of 80 mg BID orally and apart for 4 h can achieve ideal efficiency, what more important is that this regimen can greatly improve patients’ tolerance.23 Using pharmacokinetic modeling, investigators established that oral administration of abexinostat at 80 mg BID with a 4-h interval achieves sustained therapeutic exposure necessary for tumor cell eradication while limiting high peak plasma levels.23

The primary endpoint of this study was successfully achieved, indicating that abexinostat exhibits both promising efficacy and a manageable safety profile in r/r FL patients. The IRC-assessed ORR was 69.5% (57/82, 95% CI 58.4–79.2), aligning with the promising outcomes observed in previous phase I/Ⅱ studies. The ORR was 64.3% (9/14, 95% CI 35.1–87.2) for abexinostat among r/r FL patients in the Study 0403.26 The ORR was 56% (9/16, 95% CI 30–80) for abexinostat among r/r FL patients in the Study 1401.27

Abexinostat has shown efficacy in heavily pre-treated B-cell NHL due to several key factors that differentiate it from other HDAC inhibitors. One major advantage of abexinostat is its broad-spectrum activity, inhibiting a wide range of HDAC enzymes.28 This advantage allows abexinostat to impact a broader array of cancer cell survival mechanisms and epigenetic regulation pathways, which is particularly effective in the context of lymphomas that no longer respond adequately to prior lines of therapy.28

For patients with FL receiving third-line or later-line therapy, available treatment options include bispecific antibodies (mosunetuzumab and epcoritamab), chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy (axicabtagene ciloleucel, tisagenlecleucel, and lisocabtagene maraleucel), the EZH2 inhibitor tazemetostat, and regimens combining a Bruton’s tyrosine kinase inhibitor with a CD20 mAb, such as zanubrutinib plus obinutuzumab.29 For bispecific antibodies, mosunetuzumab achieved an ORR of 80% (72/90, 95% CI 70.3–87.7) with the median PFS of 17.9 months (95% CI 10.1–NR),30 while epcoritamab demonstrated an ORR of 82% (105/128, 95% CI 74.3–88.3) and the 18-month PFS rate of 49.4% (95% CI 39.0–59.1).31 For CAR T-cell therapies, the ORR was 94% (119/127, 95% CI 88-97) for axicabtagene ciloleucel,32,33 86.2% (81/94, 95% CI 77.5–92.4) for tisagenlecleucel,34 and 97% (98/101, 95% CI 91.6–99.4) for lisocabtagene maraleucel.35 The ORR of tazemetostat was 69% (31/45, 95% CI 53–82) in EZH2 mutation r/r FL patients and 35% (19/54, 95% CI 23–49) in EZH2 wild type r/r FL patients, and the median PFS was 13.8 months (95% CI 10.7–22.0) in EZH2 mutation r/r FL patients and 11.1 months (3.7–14.6) in EZH2 wild type r/r FL patients.36 The ORR was 69% (100/145, 95% CI 61–76) for zanubrutinib plus obinutuzumab, while 46% (33/72, 95% CI 34–58) for obinutuzumab monotherapy in the third-line treatment of FL patients (p = 0.001).37 Zanubrutinib in combination with obinutuzumab significantly prolonged PFS compared to obinutuzumab monotherapy (median 28.0 months [95% CI 16.1–NE] vs 10.4 months [95% CI 6.5–13.8], respectively), with a HR of 0.50 (95% CI 0.33–0.75, p < 0.001).37 Among r/r FL patients, the TRS005, a CD20 antibody-drug conjugate, demonstrated an ORR of 21.4% (3/14).38 while the fusion protein amulirafusp alfa, which combines a CD20 mAb with the CD47-binding domain of signal-regulatory protein alpha, achieved an ORR of 41.2% (7/17, 95% CI 18.4–67.1).39 In this study, the ORR was 69.5% (57/82, 95% CI 58.4–79.2) and the median PFS was 13.80 months (95% CI 9.69–30.26) for abexinostat monotherapy, showing promising efficacy compared with above mentioned treatments. Furthermore, studies showed that HDAC inhibitors could decrease cytokine release by monocytes, macrophages, and airway epithelial cells 40,41, which offers a chance for abexinostat to be combined with bispecific antibody or CAR T-cell therapy.

Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) is one of the most significant safety concerns associated with bispecific antibody and CAR T-cell therapy.30–32,34,35 The incidence of CRS was 44% (40/90) for mosunetuzumab,30 49% (42/86) for epcoritamab,31 78% (97/124) for axicabtagene ciloleucel,32 48.5% (47/97) for tisagenlecleucel,34 58% (75/130) for lisocabtagene maraleucel35 in FL patients, while all were predominantly grade 1–2, with the incidence of 2% (2/90), 2% (2/128), 6% (8/124), 0 (0/97), and 1% (1/130) for ≥ grade 3, respectively.30–32,34,35 The most common ≥ grade 3 adverse events (AEs) were neutropenia for the 2 bispecific antibodies and the three CAR-T cell therapies, with the incidence of 27% (24/90), 25% (32/128), 27% (34/124), 32.0% (31/97), and 58% (76/130), respectively.30–32,34,35 For tazemetostat, the most frequently observed treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) of ≥ grade 3 included thrombocytopenia (3/99, 3%), neutropenia (3/99, 3%), and anemia (2/99, 2%) among FL patients.36 Among patients with FL receiving zanubrutinib plus obinutuzumab, the most frequently reported AEs of any grade included thrombocytopenia (51/143, 36%), neutropenia (42/143, 29%), diarrhea (26/143, 18%), and fatigue (22/143, 15%).37 Among patients with B-cell NHL, of whom 22 had FL, neutropenia represented the most common ≥ grade 3 AE of TRS005 (19/48, 39.6%).38 Among patients with B-cell NHL receiving amulirafusp alfa (including 20 with FL), the most frequently ≥ grade 3 TRAEs included reductions in lymphocyte counts (28/48, 58.3%), white blood cell counts (10/48, 20.8%), and absolute neutrophil counts (9/48, 18.8%), as well as anemia (5/48, 10.4%).39 The safety results of this study showed that hematologic toxicities were the most common AEs of abexinostat, with thrombocytopenia being the most prevalent. The reversible nature of the hematologic AEs, especially thrombocytopenia, presents a manageable safety profile, ensuring that treatment can be sustained over longer periods with appropriate management.

This study was limited by having a single-arm, non-randomized design, which may introduce selection bias, as well as by the inclusion of only Chinese patients. Therefore, caution should be taken when explaining the results of this study.

In conclusion, the results of this study demonstrated that abexinostat had promising efficacy and manageable safety profile, supporting abexinostat as a new treatment option for the third-line or later-line treatment of r/r FL. An ongoing phase Ib/III trial (CTR20240881) is assessing the efficacy and safety of the combination of abexinostat with lenalidomide and rituximab versus the current standard of care in r/r FL patients previously treated with at least one regimen containing rituximab or other CD20 mAbs.

sec.title: Study design and patients
sec.p: This multi-center, single-arm, pivotal phase 2 study (NCT03934567) was conducted in patients with r/r FL. Eligible patients were aged ≥18 years who were expected to have a life expectancy of >3 months. Patients were required to have pathological diagnosis of grade 1, 2, or 3a FL confirmed at central laboratory based on biopsy within two years before enrollment and had received at least two lines of standard systemic treatment for FL, including anti-CD20 mAbs and cytotoxic agents. The latest treatment regimen must have disease progression during or post-treatment. Patients were required to have at least one measurable lesion by computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 to 2. Inclusion criteria specified adequate baseline blood cell counts and acceptable organ function. Renal eligibility required either a creatinine clearance ≥50 mL/min or a serum creatinine value ≤ 1.5 × ULN. Coagulation parameters were considered acceptable if the international normalized ratio was ≤1.5, with prothrombin time or activated partial thromboplastin time maintained within ≤1.5 × ULN. Liver function thresholds differed according to hepatic involvement: alanine and aspartate aminotransferase levels were required to be ≤2.5 × ULN in patients without liver involvement and ≤5 × ULN in those with liver involvement, while total bilirubin was limited to ≤1.5 × ULN. In addition, Fertile women and men were mandated to employ reliable contraceptive measures throughout treatment and for 90 days following the final administration of abexinostat.

The study protocol, informed consent form, and other relevant documents were approved by the ethics committee of National Cancer Center/Cancer Hospital, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences & Peking Union Medical College (Approval No.2021011915572502) and all the independent ethics committee or the institutional review board at each participating hospital before the study was conducted. The study protocol conformed to Declaration of Helsinki, ethical guidelines of the International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use, and local regulations. All patients signed the informed consent form before screening.

sec.title: Treatment procedures
sec.p: Abexinostat was administered orally at 80 mg BID, with doses separated by a 4-h interval, for 7 consecutive days followed by a 7-day washout period within each 28-day treatment cycle. Treatment continued until study discontinuation for any of the following reasons: disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, withdrawal at the discretion of the patient or investigator, loss to follow-up, death, or study termination.

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: The primary endpoint was ORR assessed by IRC. Secondary endpoints encompassed DCR, DoR, PFS, OS, and safety. Exploratory endpoints were the efficacy and safety of abexinostat across different FL genetic expression profiles. Efficacy assessment was conducted according to the Lugano 2014 criteria.42 Baseline tumor evaluations were completed within 28 days prior to study treatment initiation, using enhanced CT scans covering the whole body, including neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, and any other areas with known disease. During the study treatment, tumor assessments were conducted every 8 weeks within the first 24 weeks, and subsequently every 12 weeks, employing the same imaging techniques as at baseline. Positron emission tomography computed tomography evaluations were scheduled at baseline, 12-week, 24-week, and in patients who achieved CR by CT or MRI scans, to provide detailed insights into both the metabolic activity and anatomical status of tumors. For patients with suspected or confirmed disease progression, or when clinical symptoms indicate potential central nervous system involvement, brain MRI scans were performed. AEs were assessed and classified using the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0.43

The FAS comprised patients with documented exposure to abexinostat, at least two prior systemic treatment lines, and evaluable post-treatment efficacy data. The SS included patients with abexinostat exposure and available safety assessment records.

This study will be completed two years after finishing the study treatment of the last enrolled patient. If patients had not reached disease progression by the end of this study, upon assessment by the investigator and with the patient’s consent, the sponsor would continue to provide abexinostat until the investigator deemed no further benefit, or the patient requested treatment discontinuation.

With patient consent, during the screening period, patients could opt to provide tumor tissue sample biopsied within two years before enrollment to the central laboratory for biomarker analysis of CREBBP and KMT2D. The expression of these proteins will be assessed through IHC. Tumor samples could be formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue blocks or unstained slides. If no recent archived tumor tissue samples were available, a fresh tumor biopsy could be performed during the screening period. Before the first dose of abexinostat on day 1 of cycle 1, a whole blood sample was required. Upon disease progression, patients could choose to provide either a whole blood sample or a tumor biopsy for further biomarker analysis.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: This study employed a Simon two-stage design, planning to perform an interim efficacy analysis after 37 patients completed a 24-week efficacy evaluation. If less than 12 patients achieved objective response assessed by IRC at the first stage, this study could be terminated due to insufficient efficacy. Otherwise, the study will proceed to the second stage.

An ORR of ≤30% was predefined as indicating minimal clinical benefit (null hypothesis), whereas an ORR > 30% was classified as effective (alternative hypothesis). Accounting for an anticipated 15% dropout, the study aimed to enroll 96 patients, which would provide more than 80% power to reject the null hypothesis at a 0.05 significance level.

The two-sided 95% CI of ORR was calculated using Clopper-Pearson exact method. When the lower limit of 95% CI of ORR estimated from the final result is >30%, and the estimated value of ORR is ≥45%, it is considered valid. Median DoR, PFS, and OS, as well as their 95% CIs were analyzed using Kaplan-Meier method. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize laboratory tests, vital signs, electrocardiograms, and other safety indicators.
